```{r}
### Question 2
###
### R has a built in matrix solver, we are looking to solve the expected value
### /expected number of steps until we reach an absorbing state/conversion.
###
```


```{r}
### Creation of the Absorbing Finite Markov Chain
### Priors
### I = 1x9
### MRn = 9x9
### We are also sticking to first order Markov Chains for a single primary 
### purpose. 
### That being the possibility of over fitting our data. The primary goal of 
### statistics is to use finite data to create a model that can infer valuable
### information from the population. By using a higher order Markov chain that
### uses information before the single previous transition. There is a risk that
### we begin creating a model that is not only more computationally demanding.
### But is also primed to be able to predict our specific data set a lot better.
### This is despite the proprietary use of training data. Because although we
### can randomize the training data to test our model. At the end of the day we
### want a model that does the job of predicting real events not just 
### events constructed by the training data. This requires a model that powerfully
### predicts our currently available information, but also allows for a flexible 
### enough model to allow for exceptions.
```

```{r}

### Journey Filtration
train_conversion = journeys %>%
  filter(conversion == 1)
### From here, we will begin estimating P(Xt+1 = j|Xt = i, eventual conversion)
### Whilst Model 1 addresses conversion propensity 
### Model 2 addresses the expected remaining journey length conditional upon
### conversion occurring.
```

```{r}
### State Space Concatenation
channel_states <- c(
  "Direct",
  "Email Marketing",
  "Facebook",
  "Google Display",
  "Google Search",
  "Instagram",
  "Organic",
  "Youtube"
)

states <- c(
  channel_states,
  "Conversion"
)
```

```{r}
### Transition Element Calculations
train_transitions <- train_conversion %>%
  group_by(
    user_id,
    session_id
  ) %>%
  arrange(
    order,
    .by_group = TRUE
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    next_state = lead(channel)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    next_state = if_else(
      is.na(next_state),
      "Conversion",
      next_state
    )
  ) %>%
  ungroup()
```

```{r}
transition_counts <- train_transitions %>%
  count(
    channel,
    next_state,
    name = "n"
  )
transition_probs <- transition_counts %>%
  group_by(channel) %>%
  mutate(
    probability = n / sum(n)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()
```

```{r}
P <- matrix(
  0,
  nrow = length(states),
  ncol = length(states),
  dimnames = list(
    states,
    states
  )
)

for (i in seq_len(nrow(transition_probs))) {

  from <- transition_probs$channel[i]
  to   <- transition_probs$next_state[i]

  P[from, to] <-
    transition_probs$probability[i]
}
```

```{r}
### Explicitly Creating The Absorbing States
P["Conversion", ] <- 0

P[
  "Conversion",
  "Conversion"
] <- 1
### Meaning, once the conversion is reached, it remains converted.
```

```{r}
round(
  rowSums(P),
  10
)
```
```{r}
### Final Markov Object
customer_mc <- new(
  "markovchain",
  states = states,
  transitionMatrix = P,
  name = "Conditional Customer Conversion Journey"
)

customer_mc
```
```{r}
############################################################
# 4.1 - Expected Number of Steps
############################################################
###
### N = (I-Q)^-1
### 
### N = Fundamental matrix. Its entries give the expected number of visits
### to transient state j, starting from transient state i, before absorption.
### I = Identity matrix
### Q = Transient to transient transition matrix. Its the part of the full 
### transition matrix P containing probabilities of moving between transient 
### states. 
Q <- P[
  channel_states,
  channel_states
]

I8 <- diag(
  nrow(Q)
)

N <- solve(
  I8 - Q
)
```

```{r}
### Calculating The Expected Number of Steps
expected_steps <- as.numeric(
  N %*% rep(
    1,
    nrow(Q)
  )
)

names(expected_steps) <-
  rownames(Q)

expected_steps
```

```{r}
### Converts Results into Useful Display
expected_steps_table <-
  tibble(
    channel =
      names(expected_steps),

    expected_steps_to_conversion =
      expected_steps
  ) %>%
  arrange(
    expected_steps_to_conversion
  )

expected_steps_table
```

```{r}
############################################################
# 4.2 - Customer Lifecycle Stages
############################################################
###
### Determine life cycle cutoffs using TRAINING information
### only to avoid information leakage.
stage_cutoffs <- quantile(
  expected_steps,
  probs = c(
    1 / 3,
    2 / 3
  ),
  na.rm = TRUE
)

stage_cutoffs
### Deriving cutoffs from the training data. Where we divide the distribution
### of predicted remaining steps into thirds.
```


```{r}
### Assigning Channels to Each Lifestyle Stage
channel_lifecycle <-
  expected_steps_table %>%
  mutate(
    lifecycle_stage =
      case_when(

        expected_steps_to_conversion <=
          stage_cutoffs[1] ~
          "Late",

        expected_steps_to_conversion <=
          stage_cutoffs[2] ~
          "Mid",

        TRUE ~
          "Early"
      )
  )

View(channel_lifecycle)
### The point here being, we are making numerically driven categorizations. 
### Here, we can see that higher expected steps to conversion channels are 
### categorized as "early" stage life cycles. The reason for this is because 
### channels with a higher expected value have more steps remaining before 
### conversion and therefore a customer in that channel is presumabely in an 
### earlier stage of their journey.
```


```{r}
### 
current_customer_state <-
  journeys %>%
  group_by(user_id) %>%
  arrange(
    desc(session_id),
    desc(order),
    .by_group = TRUE
  ) %>%
  slice(1) %>%
  ungroup()
### Creates the "current_customer_state" object which is the user's most 
### recent journey record.

current_customer_state <-
  current_customer_state %>%
  mutate(
    predicted_steps =
      expected_steps[channel]
  )
### Furthermore, we're now adding the expected number of remaining steps for 
### each user's current channel. 

current_customer_state <-
  current_customer_state %>%
  mutate(
    lifecycle_stage =
      case_when(

        conversion == 1 ~
          "Converted",

        predicted_steps <=
          stage_cutoffs[1] ~
          "Late",

        predicted_steps <=
          stage_cutoffs[2] ~
          "Mid",

        TRUE ~
          "Early"
      )
  )
### From here, we just labelled each user as one of the four life cycle stages
### based on conversion and predicted steps
View(current_customer_state)
```


```{r}
lifecycle_summary <-
  current_customer_state %>%
  count(
    lifecycle_stage
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    proportion =
      n / sum(n)
  )

lifecycle_summary

# ==========================================================
# VALIDATION
# ==========================================================

lifecycle_validation <-
  model2_predictions %>%
  mutate(
    lifecycle_stage =
      case_when(

        predicted_steps <=
          stage_cutoffs[1] ~
          "Late",

        predicted_steps <=
          stage_cutoffs[2] ~
          "Mid",

        TRUE ~
          "Early"
      )
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    lifecycle_stage = factor(
      lifecycle_stage,
      levels = c(
        "Early",
        "Mid",
        "Late"
      ),
      ordered = TRUE
    )
  )

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# Observed remaining journey length by lifecycle stage
# ----------------------------------------------------------

stage_validation_summary <-
  lifecycle_validation %>%
  group_by(
    lifecycle_stage
  ) %>%
  summarise(

    n = n(),

    mean_actual_steps =
      mean(
        actual_steps_remaining
      ),

    median_actual_steps =
      median(
        actual_steps_remaining
      ),

    sd_actual_steps =
      sd(
        actual_steps_remaining
      ),

    .groups = "drop"
  )

stage_validation_summary

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# Formal test of differences
# ----------------------------------------------------------

stage_anova <- aov(
  actual_steps_remaining ~
    lifecycle_stage,
  data =
    lifecycle_validation
)

summary(stage_anova)

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# Visual validation
# ----------------------------------------------------------

ggplot(
  lifecycle_validation,
  aes(
    x = lifecycle_stage,
    y = actual_steps_remaining
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title =
      "Actual Remaining Journey Length by Lifecycle Stage",
    x =
      "Predicted Customer Lifecycle Stage",
    y =
      "Actual Steps Remaining Until Conversion"
  )
```
